# Final Report: Longitudinal Actigraphy and Pubertal Sleep Evaluation Study (LAPSES)

**Funder:** NIH/NICHD (K01 HD999999)
**Project Period:** July 1, 2021 – June 30, 2026
**Principal Investigator:** Marston Vancura, Ph.D.

## 1. Project Overview
The LAPSES project was a three-year longitudinal observational study designed to track changes in sleep duration, timing, and regularity across early adolescence. The study focused on adolescents residing in rural and semi-rural districts, a population historically underrepresented in pediatric sleep research. The primary aims were to quantify observed cohort changes in sleep regularity and to test associations between sleep regularity, depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), and body mass index (BMI) z-scores.

## 2. Methodology and Sample
- **Participants:** We recruited a baseline cohort of 412 adolescents (ages 12–14 at baseline; 52% female) from 8 rural and semi-rural school districts in Oakhaven County.
- **Data Collection:** Data were collected in 3 annual waves (Wave 1: Fall 2022; Wave 2: Fall 2023; Wave 3: Fall 2024). At each wave, participants wore wrist actigraphs (ActiGraph GT9X Link) on their non-dominant wrist for 14 consecutive days and nights.
- **School Schedules:** All three waves featured fully in-person attendance with standard school start times. Because data collection followed a single birth cohort across three calendar years, developmental changes and calendar-period effects cannot be cleanly separated; results represent observed cohort changes rather than purely pubertal development.
- **Retention:** Wave 2 participation was n = 381. We achieved an 84% retention rate at Wave 3 (n = 346), yielding 1,139 usable participant-waves.
- **Data Yield and Scoring:** Across the three waves, we collected a total of 13,415 valid nights of actigraphy. Participants averaged 11.8 valid nights per completed wave. Data were collected in 60-second epochs and scored using the Cole-Kripke algorithm. Nonwear was defined as >60 minutes of consecutive zero activity during daytime hours; to protect prolonged sleep immobility from being classified as nonwear, the principal sleep interval was first masked using concurrent daily sleep diaries and visual inspection of activity records. A valid night required >10 hours of wear time per 24-hour period, regardless of whether the principal sleep interval was fully captured, and a valid wave required a minimum of 7 such days. Naps were identified via sleep diaries and sustained inactivity. Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) was calculated using paired observed epochs exactly 24 hours apart, incorporating daytime naps. Because missing epoch pairs were simply excluded from the SRI denominator, our regularity estimates are subject to selective coverage biases, and the 11.8-night yield overestimates the true 24-hour continuous coverage. All reported yields and estimates derive from this processing configuration.
- **Measures:** Mood was assessed via the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Height and weight were measured objectively by trained research assistants at the schools to calculate BMI z-scores. Socioeconomic status (parental education and household income) was collected via parent surveys. Physical activity (moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, MVPA) was derived from daytime actigraphy.
- **Analysis:** We utilized multilevel mixed-effects models to separate within-person from between-person associations, employing Satterthwaite approximations for degrees of freedom. Analyses adjusted for concurrent MVPA.

## 3. Key Results
- **Sleep Duration:** Average objective sleep duration declined by 22 minutes per year across the three waves (95% CI 18–26 minutes, p < .001).
- **Sleep Regularity:** The Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) averaged 72.4 (SD 8.1) at baseline and showed a significant linear decrease of 3.1 points per year (95% CI 2.2–4.0, n = 412, obs = 1,139). Adolescents with early school start times (<8:00 AM) exhibited an additional 1.5-point annual SRI decline (95% CI 0.6–2.4) compared to those with later start times.
- **Mood Associations:** Within-person longitudinal analyses revealed that a 10-point decrease in SRI was associated with a 2.4-point increase in PHQ-9 scores (95% CI 1.1–3.7, p < .001, df = 725), independent of total sleep duration.
- **BMI Associations:** 
  - *Baseline Cross-Sectional:* In a cross-sectional analysis of the baseline sample (n = 412), short sleep duration (<7 hours average, n = 85) was associated with a +0.42 higher BMI z-score (95% CI 0.15–0.69) compared to those sleeping >8 hours (n = 142), adjusted for socioeconomic status and MVPA.
  - *Longitudinal:* In mixed-effects analyses across all three waves (n = 412, obs = 1,139), lower SRI was independently associated with higher BMI z-scores over time (+0.18 per 10-point SRI decrease, 95% CI 0.05–0.31), adjusted for concurrent MVPA.

## 4. Limitations and Gaps
While LAPSES successfully linked sleep regularity to BMI z-scores, a major limitation of the study—and of our lab's current capacity—is the complete absence of blood pressure or metabolic measurement experience. The existing LAPSES cohort data contains no blood pressure, heart rate variability, fasting glucose, or lipid panels. Furthermore, the PI and the laboratory currently have no experience, equipment, or trained personnel to conduct cardiovascular or metabolic assessments. The study was strictly observational; we have not tested any behavioral interventions to extend sleep or improve regularity.

**Vancura, M., & Arislow, C. (2026). Longitudinal declines in sleep regularity during early adolescence: The LAPSES cohort.** *Pediatric Sleep Science*, 14(2), 112-125. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2026.1

**Vancura, M., Mercator, J., & Rostovich, E. (2025). Day-to-day sleep variability and depressive symptoms in rural youth.** *Developmental Behavioral Medicine*, 29(4), 401-415. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2025.1
*Abstract:* We examined the within-person associations between day-to-day sleep variability and depressive symptoms using data from the Longitudinal Actigraphy and Pubertal Sleep Evaluation Study (LAPSES). Across 13,415 valid nights of actigraphy, we found that periods of high intra-individual variability in sleep onset and offset were concurrently associated with elevated PHQ-9 scores. Specifically, a 10-point decrease in the Sleep Regularity Index was associated with a 2.4-point increase in depressive symptoms (95% CI 1.1–3.7). Interventions targeting sleep regularity may offer a novel pathway for adolescent depression prevention.

**Mercator, J., & Vancura, M. (2024). Objective short sleep duration and BMI z-scores in a rural middle school sample.** *Adolescent Health Research*, 8(1), 45-53. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2024.1
*Abstract:* Pediatric obesity is a major public health concern, particularly in rural communities. This cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from 412 adolescents investigated the link between actigraphy-derived sleep duration and objectively measured BMI z-scores. Adolescents averaging less than 7 hours of sleep per night (n = 85) exhibited a +0.42 higher BMI z-score (95% CI 0.15–0.69) compared to those sleeping over 8 hours (n = 142). The association remained robust after controlling for socioeconomic status (parental education and income) and actigraphy-derived moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.

*Abstract:* Collecting objective sleep data in rural, under-resourced school districts presents unique logistical challenges. This paper details the recruitment, deployment, and data recovery protocols developed for a large-scale actigraphy study in Oakhaven County. We discuss strategies for maximizing device wear-time, managing lost devices, and coordinating with school administrators. The effect was partially mediated by self-reported daytime sleepiness (indirect effect −0.15, 95% CI −0.25 to −0.05).

*Abstract:* This review synthesizes current literature on the environmental factors influencing adolescent sleep hygiene, focusing on bedroom media access, parental rule-setting, and ambient light exposure. # Facilities, Resources, and Team

## Laboratory Facilities
The Adolescent Chronobiology and Development Lab (ACDL), directed by Dr. Marston Vancura, occupies 1,200 sq ft of dedicated research space in the Department of Psychology at the University of Oakhaven. The lab includes a reception area, two private assessment rooms for interviews and anthropometric measurements, a secure data processing room, and workspace for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. 

**Equipment:**
The lab is heavily equipped for objective behavioral sleep measurement. We currently own and maintain 150 ActiGraph GT9X Link monitors and 50 Philips Respironics Actiwatch 2 devices. We possess the necessary initialization hubs, charging stations, and proprietary software (ActiLife for the ActiGraph devices; Actiware for the Actiwatch 2 devices) for high-throughput data processing.

**Equipment Gaps:**
The lab is strictly equipped for behavioral and actigraphic data collection. We do not have blood pressure cuffs, ambulatory blood pressure monitors, Holter monitors, or phlebotomy capabilities. We have no clinical trial infrastructure and no staff trained in clinical cardiovascular or metabolic assessments.

## Computing Resources
The lab houses 4 high-performance workstations dedicated to actigraphy data scoring and statistical modeling. Data are stored on the University of Oakhaven's secure, HIPAA-compliant server, which features automated nightly backups and multi-factor authentication access.

## Personnel
- **Marston Vancura, Ph.D. (Principal Investigator):** Oversees all lab operations, grant administration, and statistical modeling.
- **Calla Arislow, M.S. (Lab Manager):** Manages IRB protocols, school district relationships, device inventory, and undergraduate research assistants.
- **Jolyon Mercator, Ph.D. (Postdoctoral Fellow):** Specializes in the intersection of sleep and weight status; leads the processing of raw actigraphy files.
- **Graduate Students:** Two full-time Ph.D. students in Developmental Psychology assist with data collection and literature reviews.

## Collaborations
- **Dr. Elara Rostovich (Biostatistics, University of Oakhaven):** Provides formal statistical consulting for longitudinal mixed-effects modeling.
- **Dr. Thalenor Veskareth (Cardiology, Oakhaven Medical Center):** Dr. Veskareth serves as an informal sounding board for our theoretical models linking sleep to cardiometabolic risk. However, this relationship is strictly informal. Dr. Veskareth is not a co-investigator, we have no joint publications or shared funding, and there is no letter of support from him for any current or planned grant applications.

# Summary of Community Engagement in Rural Oakhaven County

**Date:** August 15, 2026
**Prepared by:** Adolescent Chronobiology and Development Lab

## Overview
Over the past five years, our laboratory has established deep ties with the rural and semi-rural communities surrounding the University of Oakhaven. Because our research relies on high participation rates from local families, we have prioritized community engagement, co-design of recruitment materials, and sustained partnerships with local institutions.

## School District Partnerships
We currently maintain active Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with 8 rural school districts in Oakhaven County. These partnerships were instrumental in the success of the LAPSES cohort. We work directly with school nurses and physical education teachers to integrate our sleep education materials into their existing curricula. In return, the schools facilitate our recruitment assemblies and provide private spaces for our baseline anthropometric assessments.

## Clinic Partnerships and Usability Work
To understand the broader health context of our participants, we have recently partnered with 2 federally qualified health centers (FQHCs) that serve the county's under-resourced populations. 

In Spring 2026, we conducted usability work with clinic staff at these FQHCs to design strategies for deploying brief sleep-screening questionnaires in community waiting rooms. This involved iterative co-design sessions with 12 nurses and medical assistants to identify barriers to data collection in fast-paced, under-resourced clinical settings. The primary barriers identified were low health literacy among patients and the lack of integration with the clinics' electronic health record (EHR) systems.

## Focus Groups
To ensure our research questions align with community priorities, we conducted a series of focus groups in late 2025 involving 45 parents and teens from the local area. Discussions centered on barriers to healthy behaviors in rural settings. Parents consistently cited long bus commutes, lack of safe outdoor spaces for physical activity, and the stress of agricultural work schedules as major disruptors to family sleep routines.

## Future Directions in Community Engagement
Our established network of schools and FQHCs provides a robust foundation for future observational and formative research. We are uniquely positioned to conduct community-based data linkage and usability testing for new health monitoring strategies, provided we partner with clinicians who possess the medical expertise that our behavioral lab currently lacks.

# Final Report: Longitudinal Actigraphy and Mood in Pubertal Students (LAMPS)

**Funder:** NIH/NICHD (K01 HD999999)
**Project Period:** July 1, 2018 – June 30, 2023
**Principal Investigator:** Marcus Vance, Ph.D.

## 1. Project Overview
The LAMPS project was a three-year longitudinal observational study designed to track changes in sleep duration, timing, and regularity across early adolescence. The study focused on adolescents residing in rural and semi-rural districts, a population historically underrepresented in pediatric sleep research. The primary aims were to quantify the naturalistic decline in sleep regularity during pubertal development and to test longitudinal associations between sleep regularity, depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), and body mass index (BMI) z-scores.

## 2. Methodology and Sample
- **Participants:** We recruited a baseline cohort of 412 adolescents (ages 12–14 at baseline; 52% female) from 8 rural and semi-rural school districts in Oakhaven County.
- **Data Collection:** Data were collected in 3 annual waves (Wave 1: Fall 2019; Wave 2: Fall 2020; Wave 3: Fall 2021). At each wave, participants wore wrist actigraphs (ActiGraph GT9X Link) for 14 consecutive days and nights.
- **Retention:** Wave 2 participation was n = 381. We achieved an 84% retention rate at Wave 3 (n = 346), yielding 1,139 usable participant-waves.
- **Data Yield and Scoring:** Across the three waves, we collected a total of 13,415 valid nights of actigraphy. Participants averaged 11.8 valid nights per completed wave. Data were scored using the Cole-Kripke algorithm, with nonwear defined as >60 minutes of consecutive zero activity.
- **Measures:** Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) was calculated based on the probability of being in the same state (asleep/awake) at any two time-points 24 hours apart. Mood was assessed via the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Height and weight were measured objectively by trained research assistants at the schools to calculate BMI z-scores.
- **Analysis:** We utilized multilevel mixed-effects models to separate within-person from between-person associations, employing Satterthwaite approximations for degrees of freedom.

## 3. Key Results
- **Sleep Duration:** Average objective sleep duration declined by 22 minutes per year across the three waves (95% CI 18–26 minutes, p < .001).
- **Sleep Regularity:** The Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) averaged 72.4 (SD 8.1) at baseline and showed a significant linear decrease of 3.1 points per year (95% CI 2.2–4.0, n = 412, obs = 1,139). Adolescents with early school start times (<8:00 AM) exhibited an additional 1.5-point annual SRI decline (95% CI 0.6–2.4) compared to those with later start times.
- **Mood Associations:** Within-person analyses revealed that a 10-point decrease in SRI was associated with a 2.4-point increase in PHQ-9 scores (95% CI 1.1–3.7, p < .001, df = 725), independent of total sleep duration.
- **BMI Associations:** Short sleep duration (<7 hours average) was associated with a +0.42 BMI z-score (95% CI 0.15–0.69) compared to those sleeping >8 hours. Lower SRI was also independently associated with higher BMI z-scores (+0.18 per 10-point SRI decrease, 95% CI 0.05–0.31).

## 4. Limitations and Gaps
While LAMPS successfully linked sleep regularity to BMI z-scores, a major limitation of the study—and of our lab's current capacity—is the complete absence of blood pressure or metabolic measurement experience. We collected basic anthropometrics (height/weight) but did not collect blood pressure, heart rate variability, fasting glucose, or lipid panels. The PI and the laboratory currently have no experience, equipment, or trained personnel to conduct cardiovascular or metabolic assessments. Furthermore, the study was strictly observational; we have not tested any behavioral interventions to extend sleep or improve regularity.

# Selected Publications

**Vance, M., & Aris, C. (2023). Longitudinal declines in sleep regularity during early adolescence: The LAMPS cohort.** *Journal of Pediatric Sleep*, 14(2), 112-125. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2023.1
*Abstract:* Sleep regularity is increasingly recognized as a critical dimension of sleep health, yet its developmental trajectory during puberty remains poorly characterized. In a longitudinal cohort of 412 rural adolescents, we utilized 14-day wrist actigraphy across three annual waves to calculate the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI). Results indicated a baseline mean SRI of 72.4, which declined by an average of 3.1 points annually (95% CI 2.2–4.0). This decline was more pronounced in adolescents with early school start times, who showed an additional 1.5-point annual decline (95% CI 0.6–2.4). The findings highlight early adolescence as a period of significant destabilization in sleep-wake patterns, independent of total sleep duration.

**Vance, M., Mercer, J., & Rostova, E. (2022). Day-to-day sleep variability and depressive symptoms in rural youth.** *Developmental Behavioral Medicine*, 29(4), 401-415. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2022.1
*Abstract:* We examined the within-person associations between day-to-day sleep variability and depressive symptoms using data from the Longitudinal Actigraphy and Mood in Pubertal Students (LAMPS) study. Across 13,415 valid nights of actigraphy, we found that periods of high intra-individual variability in sleep onset and offset were concurrently associated with elevated PHQ-9 scores. Specifically, a 10-point decrease in the Sleep Regularity Index was associated with a 2.4-point increase in depressive symptoms (95% CI 1.1–3.7). Interventions targeting sleep regularity may offer a novel pathway for adolescent depression prevention.

**Mercer, J., & Vance, M. (2021). Objective short sleep duration and BMI z-scores in a rural middle school sample.** *Adolescent Health Research*, 8(1), 45-53. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2021.1
*Abstract:* Pediatric obesity is a major public health concern, particularly in rural communities. This cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from 412 adolescents investigated the link between actigraphy-derived sleep duration and objectively measured BMI z-scores. Adolescents averaging less than 7 hours of sleep per night exhibited a +0.42 higher BMI z-score (95% CI 0.15–0.69) compared to those sleeping over 8 hours. The association remained robust after controlling for socioeconomic status and physical activity levels.

**Vance, M. (2019). Methodological considerations for deploying wrist actigraphy in rural school settings.** *Behavioral Measurement*, 12(3), 210-222. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2019.1
*Abstract:* Collecting objective sleep data in rural, under-resourced school districts presents unique logistical challenges. This paper details the recruitment, deployment, and data recovery protocols developed for a large-scale actigraphy study in Oakhaven County. We discuss strategies for maximizing device wear-time, managing lost devices, and coordinating with school administrators. Our protocols resulted in an average of 11.8 valid nights of data per 14-day deployment period, demonstrating the feasibility of high-yield objective sleep monitoring in these settings.

**Vance, M., & Jenkins, S. (2018). Evening chronotype and academic performance in eighth-grade students.** *Chronobiology in Education*, 5(2), 88-97. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2018.1
*Abstract:* The biological shift toward eveningness during puberty often conflicts with early school start times. We assessed circadian phase preference via the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ) and correlated it with standardized test scores in 250 eighth-grade students. Strong evening preference was associated with significantly lower math scores (−0.4 SD, 95% CI −0.6 to −0.2). The effect was partially mediated by self-reported daytime sleepiness (indirect effect −0.15, 95% CI −0.25 to −0.05).

**Vance, M. (2016). Environmental determinants of sleep hygiene in early adolescence.** *Journal of Youth Development*, 22(1), 15-29. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2016.1
*Abstract:* This review synthesizes current literature on the environmental factors influencing adolescent sleep hygiene, focusing on bedroom media access, parental rule-setting, and ambient light exposure. We propose a socio-ecological model of adolescent sleep that emphasizes the interaction between biological vulnerabilities and environmental permissiveness.

# Final Report: Longitudinal Actigraphy and Mood in Pubertal Students (LAMPS)

**Funder:** NIH/NICHD (K01 HD999999)
**Project Period:** July 1, 2018 – June 30, 2023
**Principal Investigator:** Marcus Vance, Ph.D.

## 1. Project Overview
The LAMPS project was a three-year longitudinal observational study designed to track changes in sleep duration, timing, and regularity across early adolescence. The study focused on adolescents residing in rural and semi-rural districts, a population historically underrepresented in pediatric sleep research. The primary aims were to quantify observed cohort changes in sleep regularity and to test associations between sleep regularity, depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), and body mass index (BMI) z-scores. Because data collection spanned the COVID-19 pandemic, developmental and calendar-period effects cannot be cleanly separated; results represent observed cohort changes rather than purely pubertal development.

## 2. Methodology and Sample
- **Participants:** We recruited a baseline cohort of 412 adolescents (ages 12–14 at baseline; 52% female) from 8 rural and semi-rural school districts in Oakhaven County.
- **Data Collection:** Data were collected in 3 annual waves (Wave 1: Fall 2019; Wave 2: Fall 2020; Wave 3: Fall 2021). At each wave, participants wore wrist actigraphs (ActiGraph GT9X Link) on their non-dominant wrist for 14 consecutive days and nights.
- **School Schedules:** Fall 2019 featured fully in-person attendance with standard school start times. Fall 2020 involved hybrid and remote attendance modes with flexible or delayed start times due to the pandemic. Fall 2021 saw a return to fully in-person attendance and standard schedules.
- **Retention:** Wave 2 participation was n = 381. We achieved an 84% retention rate at Wave 3 (n = 346), yielding 1,139 usable participant-waves.
- **Data Yield and Scoring:** Across the three waves, we collected a total of 13,415 valid nights of actigraphy. Participants averaged 11.8 valid nights per completed wave. Data were collected in 60-second epochs and scored using the Cole-Kripke algorithm. Nonwear was defined as >60 minutes of consecutive zero activity; to protect prolonged sleep immobility from being classified as nonwear, sleep periods were identified using concurrent daily sleep diaries and the devices' ambient light sensors. A valid night required >10 hours of wear time per 24-hour period, and a valid wave required a minimum of 7 valid nights. All reported yields and estimates derive from this processing configuration.
- **Measures:** Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) was calculated using paired observed epochs exactly 24 hours apart, incorporating daytime naps; missing intervals were excluded from the denominator. Mood was assessed via the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Height and weight were measured objectively by trained research assistants at the schools to calculate BMI z-scores. Socioeconomic status (parental education and household income) was collected via parent surveys. Physical activity (moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, MVPA) was derived from daytime actigraphy.
- **Analysis:** We utilized multilevel mixed-effects models to separate within-person from between-person associations, employing Satterthwaite approximations for degrees of freedom. Analyses adjusted for attendance mode (in-person vs. remote/hybrid).

## 3. Key Results
- **Sleep Duration:** Average objective sleep duration declined by 22 minutes per year across the three waves (95% CI 18–26 minutes, p < .001).
- **Sleep Regularity:** The Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) averaged 72.4 (SD 8.1) at baseline and showed a significant linear decrease of 3.1 points per year (95% CI 2.2–4.0, n = 412, obs = 1,139). Adolescents with early school start times (<8:00 AM) during in-person instruction exhibited an additional 1.5-point annual SRI decline (95% CI 0.6–2.4) compared to those with later start times.
- **Mood Associations:** Within-person longitudinal analyses revealed that a 10-point decrease in SRI was associated with a 2.4-point increase in PHQ-9 scores (95% CI 1.1–3.7, p < .001, df = 725), independent of total sleep duration.
- **BMI Associations:** 
  - *Baseline Cross-Sectional:* In a cross-sectional analysis of the baseline sample (n = 412), short sleep duration (<7 hours average, n = 85) was associated with a +0.42 higher BMI z-score (95% CI 0.15–0.69) compared to those sleeping >8 hours (n = 142), adjusted for socioeconomic status and MVPA.
  - *Longitudinal:* In mixed-effects analyses across all three waves (n = 412, obs = 1,139), lower SRI was independently associated with higher BMI z-scores over time (+0.18 per 10-point SRI decrease, 95% CI 0.05–0.31), adjusted for concurrent MVPA and attendance mode.

## 4. Limitations and Gaps
While LAMPS successfully linked sleep regularity to BMI z-scores, a major limitation of the study—and of our lab's current capacity—is the complete absence of blood pressure or metabolic measurement experience. We collected basic anthropometrics (height/weight) but did not collect blood pressure, heart rate variability, fasting glucose, or lipid panels. The PI and the laboratory currently have no experience, equipment, or trained personnel to conduct cardiovascular or metabolic assessments. Furthermore, the study was strictly observational; we have not tested any behavioral interventions to extend sleep or improve regularity.

**Vance, M., & Aris, C. (2023). Longitudinal declines in sleep regularity during early adolescence: The LAMPS cohort.** *Journal of Pediatric Sleep*, 14(2), 112-125. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2023.1
*Abstract:* Sleep regularity is increasingly recognized as a critical dimension of sleep health. In a longitudinal cohort of 412 rural adolescents, we utilized 14-day wrist actigraphy across three annual waves (Fall 2019 to Fall 2021) to calculate the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI). Results indicated a baseline mean SRI of 72.4, which declined by an average of 3.1 points annually (95% CI 2.2–4.0). This decline was more pronounced in adolescents with early school start times, who showed an additional 1.5-point annual decline (95% CI 0.6–2.4). Because data collection spanned the COVID-19 pandemic, developmental and calendar-period effects cannot be cleanly separated; these findings represent observed cohort changes during a period of significant destabilization in sleep-wake patterns, independent of total sleep duration.

**Vance, M., Mercer, J., & Rostova, E. (2022). Day-to-day sleep variability and depressive symptoms in rural youth.** *Developmental Behavioral Medicine*, 29(4), 401-415. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2022.1
*Abstract:* We examined the within-person associations between day-to-day sleep variability and depressive symptoms using data from the Longitudinal Actigraphy and Mood in Pubertal Students (LAMPS) study. Across 13,415 valid nights of actigraphy, we found that periods of high intra-individual variability in sleep onset and offset were concurrently associated with elevated PHQ-9 scores. Specifically, a 10-point decrease in the Sleep Regularity Index was associated with a 2.4-point increase in depressive symptoms (95% CI 1.1–3.7). Interventions targeting sleep regularity may offer a novel pathway for adolescent depression prevention.

**Mercer, J., & Vance, M. (2021). Objective short sleep duration and BMI z-scores in a rural middle school sample.** *Adolescent Health Research*, 8(1), 45-53. https://doi.org/10.99999/pb.adolescent-sleep-lab.2021.1
*Abstract:* Pediatric obesity is a major public health concern, particularly in rural communities. This cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from 412 adolescents investigated the link between actigraphy-derived sleep duration and objectively measured BMI z-scores. Adolescents averaging less than 7 hours of sleep per night (n = 85) exhibited a +0.42 higher BMI z-score (95% CI 0.15–0.69) compared to those sleeping over 8 hours (n = 142). The association remained robust after controlling for socioeconomic status (parental education and income) and actigraphy-derived moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.

*Abstract:* Collecting objective sleep data in rural, under-resourced school districts presents unique logistical challenges. This paper details the recruitment, deployment, and data recovery protocols developed for a large-scale actigraphy study in Oakhaven County. We discuss strategies for maximizing device wear-time, managing lost devices, and coordinating with school administrators. Our protocols resulted in an average of 11.8 valid nights of data per 14-day deployment period across three waves of data collection, demonstrating the feasibility of high-yield objective sleep monitoring in these settings.

*Abstract:* This review synthesizes current literature on the environmental factors influencing adolescent sleep hygiene, focusing on bedroom media access, parental rule-setting, and ambient light exposure. # Summary of Community Engagement in Rural Oakhaven County

**Date:** August 15, 2023
**Prepared by:** Adolescent Chronobiology and Development Lab

## Overview
Over the past five years, our laboratory has established deep ties with the rural and semi-rural communities surrounding the University of Oakhaven. Because our research relies on high participation rates from local families, we have prioritized community engagement, co-design of recruitment materials, and sustained partnerships with local institutions.

## School District Partnerships
We currently maintain active Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with 8 rural school districts in Oakhaven County. These partnerships were instrumental in the success of the LAMPS cohort. We work directly with school nurses and physical education teachers to integrate our sleep education materials into their existing curricula. In return, the schools facilitate our recruitment assemblies and provide private spaces for our baseline anthropometric assessments.

## Clinic Partnerships and Usability Work
To understand the broader health context of our participants, we have recently partnered with 2 federally qualified health centers (FQHCs) that serve the county's under-resourced populations. 

In Spring 2023, we conducted usability work with clinic staff at these FQHCs to design strategies for deploying brief sleep-screening questionnaires in community waiting rooms. This involved iterative co-design sessions with 12 nurses and medical assistants to identify barriers to data collection in fast-paced, under-resourced clinical settings. The primary barriers identified were low health literacy among patients and the lack of integration with the clinics' electronic health record (EHR) systems.

## Focus Groups
To ensure our research questions align with community priorities, we conducted a series of focus groups in late 2022 involving 45 parents and teens from the local area. Discussions centered on barriers to healthy behaviors in rural settings. Parents consistently cited long bus commutes, lack of safe outdoor spaces for physical activity, and the stress of agricultural work schedules as major disruptors to family sleep routines.

## Future Directions in Community Engagement
Our established network of schools and FQHCs provides a robust foundation for future observational and formative research. We are uniquely positioned to conduct community-based data linkage and usability testing for new health monitoring strategies, provided we partner with clinicians who possess the medical expertise that our behavioral lab currently lacks.

# Summary of Community Engagement in Rural Oakhaven County

**Date:** August 15, 2026
**Prepared by:** Adolescent Chronobiology and Development Lab

## Overview
Over the past five years, our laboratory has established deep ties with the rural and semi-rural communities surrounding the University of Oakhaven. Because our research relies on high participation rates from local families, we have prioritized community engagement, co-design of recruitment materials, and sustained partnerships with local institutions.

## School District Partnerships
We currently maintain active Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with 8 rural school districts in Oakhaven County. These partnerships were instrumental in the success of the LAPSES cohort. We work directly with school nurses and physical education teachers to integrate our sleep education materials into their existing curricula. In return, the schools facilitate our recruitment assemblies and provide private spaces for our baseline anthropometric assessments.

## Clinic Partnerships and Usability Work
To understand the broader health context of our participants, we have recently partnered with 2 federally qualified health centers (FQHCs) that serve the county's under-resourced populations. 

In Spring 2026, we conducted usability work with clinic staff at these FQHCs to design strategies for deploying brief sleep-screening questionnaires in community waiting rooms. This involved iterative co-design sessions with 12 nurses and medical assistants to identify barriers to data collection in fast-paced, under-resourced clinical settings. The primary barriers identified were low health literacy among patients and the lack of integration with the clinics' electronic health record (EHR) systems.

## Focus Groups
To ensure our research questions align with community priorities, we conducted a series of focus groups in late 2025 involving 45 parents and teens from the local area. Discussions centered on barriers to healthy behaviors in rural settings. Parents consistently cited long bus commutes, lack of safe outdoor spaces for physical activity, and the stress of agricultural work schedules as major disruptors to family sleep routines.

## Future Directions in Community Engagement
Our established network of schools and FQHCs provides a robust foundation for future observational and formative research. We are uniquely positioned to conduct community-based data linkage and usability testing for new health monitoring strategies, provided we partner with clinicians who possess the medical expertise that our behavioral lab currently lacks.

# Facilities, Resources, and Team

## Laboratory Facilities
The Adolescent Chronobiology and Development Lab (ACDL), directed by Dr. Marston Vancura, occupies 1,200 sq ft of dedicated research space in the Department of Psychology at the University of Oakhaven. The lab includes a reception area, two private assessment rooms for interviews and anthropometric measurements, a secure data processing room, and workspace for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. 

**Equipment:**
The lab is heavily equipped for objective behavioral sleep measurement. We currently own and maintain 150 ActiGraph GT9X Link monitors and 50 Philips Respironics Actiwatch 2 devices. We possess the necessary initialization hubs, charging stations, and proprietary software (ActiLife for the ActiGraph devices; Actiware for the Actiwatch 2 devices) for high-throughput data processing.

**Equipment Gaps:**
The lab is strictly equipped for behavioral and actigraphic data collection. We do not have blood pressure cuffs, ambulatory blood pressure monitors, Holter monitors, or phlebotomy capabilities. We have no clinical trial infrastructure and no staff trained in clinical cardiovascular or metabolic assessments.

## Computing Resources
The lab houses 4 high-performance workstations dedicated to actigraphy data scoring and statistical modeling. Data are stored on the University of Oakhaven's secure, HIPAA-compliant server, which features automated nightly backups and multi-factor authentication access.

## Personnel
- **Marston Vancura, Ph.D. (Principal Investigator):** Oversees all lab operations, grant administration, and statistical modeling.
- **Calla Arislow, M.S. (Lab Manager):** Manages IRB protocols, school district relationships, device inventory, and undergraduate research assistants.
- **Jolyon Mercator, Ph.D. (Postdoctoral Fellow):** Specializes in the intersection of sleep and weight status; leads the processing of raw actigraphy files.
- **Graduate Students:** Two full-time Ph.D. students in Developmental Psychology assist with data collection and literature reviews.

## Collaborations
- **Dr. Elara Rostovich (Biostatistics, University of Oakhaven):** Provides formal statistical consulting for longitudinal mixed-effects modeling.
- **Dr. Elian Thornfield (Cardiology, Oakhaven Medical Center):** Dr. Thornfield serves as an informal sounding board for our theoretical models linking sleep to cardiometabolic risk. However, this relationship is strictly informal. Dr. Thornfield is not a co-investigator, we have no joint publications or shared funding, and there is no letter of support from him for any current or planned grant applications.

# Summary of Community Engagement in Rural Oakhaven County

**Date:** August 15, 2026
**Prepared by:** Adolescent Chronobiology and Development Lab

## Overview
Over the past five years, our laboratory has established deep ties with the rural and semi-rural communities surrounding the University of Oakhaven. Because our research relies on high participation rates from local families, we have prioritized community engagement, co-design of recruitment materials, and sustained partnerships with local institutions.

## School District Partnerships
We currently maintain active Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with 8 rural school districts in Oakhaven County. These partnerships were instrumental in the success of the LAPSES cohort. We work directly with school nurses and physical education teachers to integrate our sleep education materials into their existing curricula. In return, the schools facilitate our recruitment assemblies and provide private spaces for our baseline anthropometric assessments.

## Clinic Partnerships and Usability Work
To understand the broader health context of our participants, we have recently partnered with 2 federally qualified health centers (FQHCs) that serve the county's under-resourced populations. 

In Spring 2026, we conducted usability work with clinic staff at these FQHCs to design strategies for deploying brief sleep-screening questionnaires in community waiting rooms. This involved iterative co-design sessions with 12 nurses and medical assistants to identify barriers to data collection in fast-paced, under-resourced clinical settings. The primary barriers identified were low health literacy among patients and the lack of integration with the clinics' electronic health record (EHR) systems.

## Focus Groups
To ensure our research questions align with community priorities, we conducted a series of focus groups in late 2025 involving 45 parents and teens from the local area. Discussions centered on barriers to healthy behaviors in rural settings. Parents consistently cited long bus commutes, lack of safe outdoor spaces for physical activity, and the stress of agricultural work schedules as major disruptors to family sleep routines.

## Future Directions in Community Engagement
Our established network of schools and FQHCs provides a robust foundation for future observational and formative research. We are uniquely positioned to conduct community-based data linkage and usability testing for new health monitoring strategies, provided we partner with clinicians who possess the medical expertise that our behavioral lab currently lacks.

facts.text: The LAPSES study recruited a baseline cohort of 412 adolescents (ages 12-14, 52% female).
Wave 3 retained 346 participants, an 84% retention rate.
The study yielded 1,139 usable participant-waves.
The project collected a total of 13,415 valid nights of actigraphy across three waves.
Participants averaged 11.8 valid nights of actigraphy per completed wave.
A valid night required >10 hours of wear time per 24-hour period, regardless of whether the principal sleep interval was fully captured.
Missing epoch pairs were simply excluded from the SRI denominator, subjecting regularity estimates to selective coverage biases.
The 11.8-night yield overestimates the true 24-hour continuous coverage.
Average objective sleep duration declined by 22 minutes per year (95% CI 18-26 minutes).
SRI showed a significant linear decrease of 3.1 points per year (95% CI 2.2-4.0).
A 10-point decrease in SRI was associated with a 2.4-point increase in PHQ-9 scores (95% CI 1.1-3.7), independent of total sleep duration.
In a baseline cross-sectional analysis, short sleep duration (<7 hours, n = 85) was associated with a +0.42 higher BMI z-score (95% CI 0.15-0.69) compared to >8 hours (n = 142).
In longitudinal mixed-effects analyses, lower SRI was independently associated with higher BMI z-scores over time (+0.18 per 10-point SRI decrease, 95% CI 0.05-0.31).
Because data collection followed a single cohort across three calendar years, developmental and calendar-period effects cannot be cleanly separated.
The existing LAPSES cohort data contains no blood pressure or metabolic measurements.
